title: In-Memory Key-Value Store
summary: A mini-Redis prompt: generic storage, TTL expiry, and pluggable persistence — broader than a cache's eviction-only focus, since nothing here is required to ever be evicted.

slides.markdown:
"Design an in-memory key-value store" is a mini-Redis prompt, and it's easy to confuse with "design a cache" — but a cache's entire job is deciding what to evict under a capacity limit, while a key-value store's job is general-purpose storage that *may* also expire or persist data. Eviction is optional here; expiry and durability are the core concerns.

Get this distinction right early: if you jump straight to an LRU eviction policy, you've answered a narrower question than the one being asked.

slides.sectionTitle: Requirements: get/set/delete, TTL expiry, pluggable persistence
slides.markdown:
The contract: **`get`/`set`/`delete`** on arbitrary keys, an optional **TTL** per key that expires it automatically, and **pluggable persistence** so data can survive a restart without that being baked into the core storage logic.

**Non-goals** to state up front: distribution and replication across machines are explicitly out of scope for this class-level design — a single process, single-machine store. That's a deliberate scoping choice, not an oversight; it's what keeps this a data-structures-and-concurrency problem rather than a distributed-systems one.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: Store, Entry, ExpiryPolicy, PersistenceStrategy
slides.markdown:
Four classes. **`Store`** is the public API — `get`/`set`/`delete` — backed internally by a hashmap. **`Entry`** wraps a stored value together with its optional expiry timestamp, so expiry data travels with the value rather than living in a separate parallel structure. **`ExpiryPolicy`** decides *when* and *how* expired entries get removed (lazy on access, active sweep, or both). **`PersistenceStrategy`** decides how the in-memory state is written to durable storage, independent of the storage logic itself.

The pattern across all four: `Store` depends on `ExpiryPolicy` and `PersistenceStrategy` as interfaces, not concrete implementations — swapping either doesn't touch `Store`'s core get/set/delete code.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the store, its entries, and pluggable expiry/persistence
slides.markdown:
![Store class diagram showing Entry composition and ExpiryPolicy/PersistenceStrategy dependencies](assets/store-class-diagram.svg)

`Store` owns the map of `Entry` objects directly, but only *depends on* the `ExpiryPolicy` and `PersistenceStrategy` interfaces — it never depends on a specific implementation of either. That's what makes both swappable independently: changing how expiry works doesn't touch how persistence works, and vice versa.

This is the same shape as the eviction-policy Strategy from the LRU cache topic, applied to two different concerns at once.

assets.alt: Store class diagram showing Entry composition and ExpiryPolicy/PersistenceStrategy dependencies

slides.sectionTitle: Code: set() with TTL, and lazy expiry check on get()
The hard part: expiring millions of keys without scanning on every access
slides.markdown:
Lazy expiry alone has a gap: a key that expires and is **never accessed again** stays in memory forever, since nothing ever triggers its removal. At millions of keys with TTLs, that's a real, unbounded memory leak, not a theoretical one.

Scanning the entire map on every `get` to check for other expired keys would fix the leak but destroys the O(1) guarantee `get` is supposed to have. The design has to separate two concerns: making a single `get` fast (lazy check, O(1), only touches the key being read) from making the *whole store* eventually reclaim expired memory (a background process, decoupled from any individual request's latency).

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: lazy expiry on access plus active sweep on a timer
slides.markdown:
![Two parallel expiry paths, lazy on access and active sweep on a timer, converging on the same removal step](assets/expiry-paths.svg)

Lazy expiry catches keys the instant someone tries to use them again — zero extra background cost, but blind to keys nobody touches. Active sweep catches exactly those forgotten keys, by periodically sampling a batch (not the whole map at once, to bound the pause) and removing anything expired.

Running both together closes the gap either leaves alone: lazy handles the hot path cheaply, active sweep bounds the worst-case memory of cold, forgotten, expired keys.

assets.alt: Two parallel expiry paths, lazy on access and active sweep on a timer, converging on the same removal step

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: lazy expiry vs active-sweep vs a min-heap of expiry times
slides.markdown:
A third option — a min-heap ordered by expiry time — trades implementation complexity for precision.

| | Lazy expiry | Active sweep (sampling) | Min-heap of expiry times |
|---|---|---|---|
| Catches forgotten keys | No — only triggers on access | Eventually — bounded by sweep interval | Immediately — always know the next key to expire |
| Cost per get() | O(1), one timestamp check | None (runs on a separate timer) | None (heap only touched on expiry, not on every get) |
| Cost to reclaim memory | Never, for untouched keys | Amortized across sweep batches | O(log n) per removal, precisely timed |
| Implementation complexity | Trivial | Simple (sample + check) | Higher — a second data structure to keep in sync with the map |

**How to decide:** lazy alone is never sufficient on its own — pair it with active sweep by default, since it's simple and bounds memory well enough for most workloads. Reach for a min-heap only when you need precise, immediate expiry (e.g. a session store where a stale session must vanish exactly on time) and can justify the extra bookkeeping.

slides.sectionTitle: Concurrency: readers and a background expiry sweep on the same map
slides.markdown:
The active sweep runs on its own thread, but it's mutating the same map that `get`/`set` calls from other threads are reading and writing concurrently — deleting a key while another thread is mid-lookup on it is a data race if the underlying map isn't safe for concurrent mutation during iteration.

The standard fix mirrors the LRU cache's thread-safety story: guard mutations with a lock fine-grained enough not to serialize every read behind the sweep (e.g. a per-shard lock, so the sweep only blocks the shard it's currently cleaning), or use a concurrent map implementation that tolerates safe iteration-while-mutating. The key discipline is the same as ever: the sweep's removal must be atomic with respect to any concurrent get on that same key, not a separate check-then-delete that a lookup can interleave with.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending to additional data types without an if/else per type
slides.markdown:
Real key-value stores (Redis included) support more than strings — lists, sets, hashes — and the naive extension is an `if value_type == "list": ... elif value_type == "set": ...` scattered through `Store`. That doesn't scale past two or three types and puts every type's logic in one class.

The cleaner extension keeps `Entry.value` as a generic slot that can hold any supported type, and pushes type-specific operations (`lpush`, `sadd`, `hset`) into separate methods or wrapper classes that operate on that value — `Store` itself stays generic over "a key maps to some value with an optional expiry," and doesn't need to know or care what operations a list value supports versus a set value.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: letting persistence writes block the main read/write path
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Every `set()` call should immediately write through to disk so we never lose data — durability first, always."

**Why it's wrong:** synchronous disk writes on every `set` couple the store's in-memory speed (its entire reason for existing) to disk I/O latency, which can be orders of magnitude slower. A key-value store meant to serve sub-millisecond reads now pays disk-write latency on every mutation, defeating its own purpose.

**Correct model:** run persistence off to the side — a periodic snapshot of the full dataset, or an append-only log written asynchronously — so the in-memory path stays fast and durability is a background concern with a bounded, known window of potential data loss (e.g. "at most the last second of writes"), not a per-call cost.
